final_proof:
We are required to prove the equivalence of two definitions of an adjunction. Both definitions agree that an adjunction involves a pair of covariant functors $F: \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ and $G: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$. They differ only in how they state the conditions on $\alpha$. 

**Definition 1 implies Definition 2:**
Assume Definition 1 holds. Thus, $\alpha$ is a natural isomorphism between the bifunctors $\map {\mathrm {Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {F-, -}$ and $\map {\mathrm {Hom}_{\mathbf D} } {-, G-}$. 

By the definition of a natural isomorphism, $\alpha$ is a natural transformation such that for every object $\tuple{D^{\mathrm{op}}, C}$ in the product category $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$, the component $\alpha_{\tuple{D^{\mathrm{op}}, C}}$ is an isomorphism in the target category $\mathbf{Set}$. 
An isomorphism in $\mathbf{Set}$ is precisely a bijection. This satisfies the condition in Definition 2 that $\alpha_{\tuple{D^{\mathrm{op}}, C}}$ is a bijection from $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {FD, C}$ to $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D} } {D, GC}$.

Furthermore, by the definition of a natural transformation, for any morphism $\tuple{f^{\mathrm{op}}, g}: \tuple{D_1^{\mathrm{op}}, C_1} \to \tuple{D_2^{\mathrm{op}}, C_2}$ in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$, the corresponding naturality square must commute. 
The morphism $f^{\mathrm{op}}: D_1^{\mathrm{op}} \to D_2^{\mathrm{op}}$ in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}$ corresponds to a morphism $f: D_2 \to D_1$ in $\mathbf D$, and $g: C_1 \to C_2$ is a morphism in $\mathbf C$.
The domain functor is the hom bifunctor with left functor, $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}} {F-, -}$, whose action on the morphism $\tuple{f^{\mathrm{op}}, g}$ is given by the mapping $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}} {Ff^{\mathrm{op}}, g}$, defined by $h \mapsto g \circ h \circ Ff$.
The codomain functor is the hom bifunctor with right functor, $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}} {-, G-}$, whose action on the same morphism is given by $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}} {f^{\mathrm{op}}, Gg}$, defined by $h \mapsto Gg \circ h \circ f$.
The naturality condition states that the composition of the functor's morphism map with the component of $\alpha$ must be equal on both paths of the square:
$$ \alpha_{\tuple{D_2^{\mathrm{op}}, C_2}} \circ \map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}} {Ff^{\mathrm{op}}, g} = \map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}} {f^{\mathrm{op}}, Gg} \circ \alpha_{\tuple{D_1^{\mathrm{op}}, C_1}} $$
This exactly matches the commutative diagram condition given in Definition 2. Thus, Definition 2 is satisfied.

**Definition 2 implies Definition 1:**
Assume Definition 2 holds. 
We are given a family of mappings $\alpha$ indexed by the objects $\tuple{D^{\mathrm{op}}, C}$ of $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$. Since each component $\alpha_{\tuple{D^{\mathrm{op}}, C}}$ is given as a bijection, it is an isomorphism in $\mathbf{Set}$. 

We are also given that for any morphisms $f^{\mathrm{op}}: D_1^{\mathrm{op}} \to D_2^{\mathrm{op}}$ in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $g: C_1 \to C_2$ in $\mathbf C$, the following diagram commutes:
$$ \alpha_{\tuple{D_2^{\mathrm{op}}, C_2}} \circ \map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}} {Ff^{\mathrm{op}}, g} = \map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}} {f^{\mathrm{op}}, Gg} \circ \alpha_{\tuple{D_1^{\mathrm{op}}, C_1}} $$
Because $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}} {Ff^{\mathrm{op}}, g}$ and $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}} {f^{\mathrm{op}}, Gg}$ are exactly the actions of the bifunctors $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}} {F-, -}$ and $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}} {-, G-}$ on the morphism $\tuple{f^{\mathrm{op}}, g}$ in $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$, this equation holding for every such morphism is precisely the requirement for $\alpha$ to be a natural transformation from $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}} {F-, -}$ to $\map {\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}} {-, G-}$.

Because $\alpha$ is a natural transformation and each of its components is an isomorphism in $\mathbf{Set}$, $\alpha$ is a natural isomorphism. 
This means $\alpha$ is a natural isomorphism between the two hom bifunctors, which perfectly satisfies Definition 1.

Since both implications hold, Definition 1 and Definition 2 are equivalent.
